sources.title: DC Compound Motor - An Overview
sources.quote: Reversing the direction of rotation of compound or stabilized – shunt motors is accomplished by reversing the armature branch or reversing both the series field and the shunt field.

notes.claim: The synchronous speed of the turning field is 120 f / p rpm for f hertz and p poles; an induction motor's shaft runs a little slower than it.
In a series motor the same current flows through field and armature, and its speed can climb to dangerous levels if it runs without a load.
A motor that is turning also acts as a generator; the emf it makes is called back emf and it opposes the supply.
Three windings 120 electrical degrees apart, each fed from one phase, make one combined magnetic field that turns at a constant speed, the synchronous speed.
The turning field cuts the short-circuited rotor conductors and induces a current in them; that current makes its own field, which interacts with the stator field to give torque.

The rotor has to turn slower than the field: with no speed difference there is no cutting, so no current is induced and no torque is produced. An induction motor can approach synchronous speed but never reach it.
Slip is the difference between synchronous and actual speed, normally written as a percentage. Load makes the rotor slow and slip grow; taking load off lets it speed up and slip shrink.
Synchronous speed is 120 f / p rpm for f hertz and p poles.
Full-load slip of a cage motor is a few percent: about 2 to 3% (one maker) and under 5% (another).
Starting from the supply direct, a motor draws usually 6 to 8 times its rated current and can draw more than 10 times.
For a small motor (up to about 30 kW) ABB's 2010 handbook gives a direct-on-line starting torque of 1.5 to 2.5 times rated; its 2004 edition gave 2.5 to 3. The figure is a range.
Swapping the supply connections on any two of the three coils reverses the field and so the direction of rotation.

A cage rotor is simple, rugged and low-maintenance, with no brushes or slip rings; a wound rotor gives higher starting torque and speed control by external resistance, at more upkeep. Light load gives a poor power factor.
Cage induction motors suit constant-speed work such as fans, pumps, conveyors and compressors; their speed is hard to control without a drive and their starting current is high.
Induction motors are used on ships for pumps, fans and compressors up to 700 kW or more, totally enclosed; the UK chose an induction motor to drive its Type 45 destroyer.
A three-phase motor run from a single phase will not self-start but can be hand started; a motor already running when one phase is lost heats very quickly and must be taken off by its protection.
In one long-run record of motor failures, overloads were 30%, single-phasing 14% and bearing failure 13%; worn starter contacts are given as the most common cause of single-phasing.

An insulation resistance test shows a wet or contaminated motor or a dead short to earth but cannot prove it good; a winding resistance test compares phases, and under 1% difference is typical of a good winding.
His sheet says a brushless motor is safe for hazardous areas; a maker builds hazardous-area motors to prevent ignition and certifies them to ATEX and IECEx.
notes.contested: Dan's sheet treats the absence of brushes as making these motors safe in hazardous areas; a maker presents certified, purpose-built motors for these areas.

notes.claim: Slip is the fraction (synchronous speed minus actual speed) divided by synchronous speed: 0 at synchronous speed, 1 (100%) at standstill or locked rotor.

Read the pole count from the nameplate speed: on 50 Hz a two-pole field turns at 3000 rpm and a four-pole one at 1500, and the full-load speed on the nameplate is a little below that. A 1500 r/min, four-pole motor is a maker's standard 50 Hz line. Dan's sheet motor, 5.5 kW at 2950 rpm, is therefore two-pole at 50 Hz (computed: slip (3000 - 2950) / 3000 = 1.67%).
The ABB 0.75 kW four-pole data sheet gives a rated speed of 1437 r/min on 50 Hz, so its full-load slip is (1500 - 1437) / 1500 = 4.2% (computed).
Slip is proportional to the load: a motor at half load has slip halfway between its full-load slip and zero.
When load goes up the rotor slows, slip grows, and rotor current and torque grow with it until the motor's torque balances the load's. At small slip the torque is directly proportional to slip.
The rotor current's frequency is slip times the supply frequency, so at full load (slip 5% or less) it is only a few hertz: 2.5 Hz on a 50 Hz supply at 5% slip.

Light-load power factor is poor because the magnetising current stays almost the same while the useful current falls. ABB's 0.75 kW four-pole motor draws 1.4 A with no load against 1.90 A at full load, with power factor 0.7 at full load and 0.49 at half load. Below about half load the power factor degrades quickly.

The ABB 0.75 kW four-pole data sheet gives a starting current of 5.9 times rated, a locked-rotor torque of 3.5 times rated and a maximum (breakdown) torque of 3.8 times rated. The starting current is high because a locked rotor is like a shorted transformer secondary.
notes.contested: Starting torque of a direct-on-line cage motor: ABB's handbook gives 1.5 to 2.5 times rated for small motors, while the small ABB data sheet gives 3.5. It is a range that depends on the motor design, so read the data sheet for the motor in hand.

notes.claim: If the load torque goes beyond the motor's breakdown torque the motor slows further instead of settling: it stalls, the current stays at the locked-rotor level, and it overheats rapidly and risks insulation failure if not protected.

With one line open at standstill the rotating field collapses into a pulsing single-phase field, so a motor at rest hums and will not start. If the motor was already running and one line is lost, the two remaining line currents rise to about 173% of normal.

The minimum acceptable insulation resistance for a motor winding depends on the standard, the winding and its age: the older IEEE 43 rule is 1 megohm plus 1 megohm per kV; a widely quoted newer figure is 5 megohms for windings up to 1,000 V (WEG, citing IEEE 43); a maker or the standard in force sets the real value, and the trend counts as much as one reading.
notes.contested: The minimum insulation resistance for a motor: the older IEEE 43 rule (1 megohm plus 1 per kV), a newer 5 megohm figure for low-voltage windings, and a note that the real minimum depends on the insulation. The lesson should send him to the maker's figure rather than state one number.

notes.claim: Royal Navy ships have used a 440 V, 60 Hz, three-phase main supply since 1946 (four Daring class destroyers, in line with US Navy practice); it has been the preferred supply ever since. So a motor at sea usually runs on 60 Hz. (Added for i1, review fix: why the 60 Hz choice matters.)

A motor's overload relay is set to the motor's rated current, not its tripping current: it does not trip at 1.05 times the setting and trips at 1.2 times. An overloaded motor draws more than its rated current until the relay trips. (Added for i1, review fix: how an overload shows and what to check.)

The isolator closes the supply; Start (normally open, sprung) makes the coil circuit; the coil pulls in the main contacts, and a latching contact across Start keeps the coil fed once Start is released.
Stop (normally closed) breaks the coil circuit, and so does the overload's release contact after its bimetal strips bend; the coil drops out and the contacts release.

The coil does the pulling and holding of the main contacts; the latching contact's job is to keep the coil fed. (His sheet's item 7 words it as the latching contacts pulling and holding the main contacts.)

After a power cut the coil drops out and the motor stops; it does not restart by itself, because the holding contact has returned to open. A contactor with a holding contact gives low-voltage protection; maintained contacts give low-voltage release.
The overload's contacts sit in series with the coil and are operated by heat, not by the contactor's movement.
Overload relays protect against overload only: fuses or a breaker give the short-circuit protection, and a maker advises fuses with the thermal overload relay.
His coil is 230 V, fed from one phase and neutral; the coil rating must be right for how it is connected and for the supply voltage.
Direct-on-line starting is uncontrolled: full current and torque from the start. Start current is usually 6 to 8 times rated and can exceed 10 times.
His sheet gives DOL up to 5 kW; the web summary gives often under 4 kW; ABB says the limit depends on the area of use, and some utilities restrict DOL starting for motors of 5.5 kW or higher.
notes.contested: Rules of thumb for the largest DOL motor differ (5 kW, under 4 kW, 5.5 kW); the maker says it depends on the area of use and gives 5.5 kW as one utility limit.

notes.claim: DOL starters are used for compressors, pumps and fans; repeated stopping and starting can make the thermal overload operate.

Star-delta cuts starting current to about 30% (a third) and starting torque to about 25% of direct-on-line; the motor must be delta connected when running, and the starter uses three contactors, an overload and a timer.
Star-delta works only when the load is light at the start, and there are current peaks at the switch from star to delta.
His group's star-delta worked answer multiplies the star power by 3 to get the delta power.
The web summary's wording that DOL gives 100% of rated torque is loose: ABB gives full starting torque as 1.5 to 2.5 times rated for a small motor.
His group handout says that start buttons are wired in parallel.
Isolate and prove dead before work on a starter: the maker's own instruction is to disconnect power before any work on the equipment.

A contactor is rated for the motor it switches: for squirrel-cage motors (duty AC-3) it makes about 6 to 8 times the rated current when closing, or 5 to 7 on another maker's figure, and breaks only the rated current when opening; most contact wear comes from the making.
Restarting a motor before it has stopped turning can give a current peak up to twice that of a start from standstill, so a quick Stop-then-Start is hard on the contacts.
A DOL starter connects the motor straight to the supply at full voltage; the start current can cause voltage dips on the supply and heavy forces in the cables and the motor windings.

On a generator supply, DOL gives the highest inrush of any starting method, and the motor can develop several times full-load torque; on a ship the generator, not the starter, is the limit, and large motors starting one after another during manoeuvring can cause severe voltage dips.

Star-delta puts each winding on 1/sqrt(3) of the line voltage while starting; the changeover can briefly open the supply and give a current spike, which on one generator maker's figures can be as high as 5 x run kVA if it is badly timed, but ABB says is typically lower than a DOL start.
notes.contested: Sources differ on the size of the star-to-delta changeover spike: ABB says typically lower than a DOL start; a generator maker warns it can reach 5 x run kVA if the changeover is not set well.

notes.claim: The overload relay is set to the motor's rated current, not its trip current: no trip at 1.05 times the setting, trip at 1.2 times; it also protects against phase failure, and it has no power contacts so it can only work through the contactor.
After an overload trip the relay will not reset until it has cooled, which lets the motor cool before it is restarted.

The contactor coil must have the right voltage: the usual limits are 0.85 to 1.1 times its rating; too low a voltage can fail to close it, make it chatter and melt the coil, and too high a voltage can burn it out.

A buzzing or chattering contactor points to low or unstable coil voltage, a poor control connection, a wrong coil, dirty or unseated magnet faces, or a damaged shading ring; check the voltage across the coil terminals while it is closing.

A contactor can hold line voltage even when its coil circuit is off, so isolate and prove dead before touching a starter: prove all supply conductors dead, with a voltage indicator that is proved before and after use.
Several Stop buttons go in series (any one stops the motor) and several Start buttons in parallel with the holding contact (any one starts it).
Some supply utilities restrict direct-on-line starting for motors rated at 5.5 kW (7.5 hp) or higher.
In a star-delta starter only 1/sqrt(3) of the motor current flows through the main (line) contactor, so an overload relay mounted on it is set to 0.58 times the motor current.
A drive has three parts: a rectifier turns AC to DC, a DC bus with capacitors smooths it, and an inverter switches it back to AC at chosen frequency and voltage by pulse-width modulation.
Motor speed follows the supply frequency, so a drive that sets the frequency sets the speed.
Voltage is lowered in proportion to frequency so the flux stays constant (constant V/f); otherwise the motor draws excessive current at low frequency, with saturation.

Below the nominal frequency is the constant flux range; above it the voltage can rise no further and the motor is in field weakening, where it can run at constant power, so maximum torque falls with frequency.
A drive's soft start removes the inrush of a direct start and the mechanical shock.
For fans and pumps power varies roughly as the cube of speed: half speed needs about one eighth power in theory; a maker says treat the savings as theoretical.
Slowing a conveyor from 100% to 80% saves 20% of energy while a pump or fan saves nearer 50%, so savings are large only on variable-torque loads.
VFDs on ships are used on cranes, winches, bow thrusters, ventilation, pumps and compressors (a maker's list).
Fast-rising voltage pulses and high switching frequencies of modern drives can send current pulses through motor bearings that erode the races.
A drive trip on over-voltage during stopping can come from regenerated energy: the fix named is a longer deceleration time or a brake chopper; harmonics can also overcharge the DC link capacitors.
Earth-fault trips are found from the sum of the output currents and often from weak or damp insulation; disconnect the drive before an insulation resistance test on the motor and cable.

Before any work on a drive, its motor or its motor cable: isolate the whole drive, wait 5 minutes for the DC bus capacitors to discharge, then measure across the DC terminals (UDC+ and UDC-) with a multimeter before starting. The isolator on the cabinet door may not remove voltage from the input busbars.

The DC bus sits at about 1.35 times the supply line voltage (1.41 times the peak of a sine supply), so a 400 V drive holds roughly 540 to 565 V DC after the supply is off, until the capacitors are discharged.
Do not start and stop the motor with the isolator; use the drive's own start and stop. Power-ups are limited (five in ten minutes on one maker's drive) to protect the capacitor charging circuit.

Check the motor and all driven equipment can run safely across the whole speed range the drive allows, which can be above or below the speed on direct supply; a motor driven faster than set by the load raises the DC bus voltage and can damage the capacitors.

A maker's list of the common drive faults: overcurrent, current limit, ground (earth) fault, output phase fault, overvoltage, undervoltage, drive over temperature, motor over temperature and input phase fault.
Overcurrent trips point to the motor and its cable: check the wiring and the motor for short circuits and earth faults, loose connections or winding faults, and a motor that is blocked or overloaded.
An input phase failure is spotted by the ripple on the DC bus, which increases when a phase is lost; the drive trips on it (a blown fuse or loose input connection is the usual cause).
A drive can be set to reset itself and carry on after a fault; where it is, the machine can restart by itself and must be labelled so.
On a 400 V drive one maker sets the DC overvoltage trip at 840 V; a brake chopper passes surplus energy from the DC bus into a brake resistor when the bus voltage rises above a set limit.

A drive's diode rectifier draws current that is not a sine wave (harmonics); the common 6-pulse bridge with no choke can have a current distortion of around 80% and a line reactor or DC choke brings it to about 35 to 50%.

On ships, variable speed drives are the main source of harmonic distortion; Lloyd's Register limits voltage distortion at a switchboard to 8% of the fundamental, and NATO warship standard STANAG 1008 limits voltage THD to 5% with no single harmonic above 3%.
A standard self-ventilated motor cools less as it slows, so the torque it can give continuously at low speed is limited; larger inverter-duty motors often have a constant-speed auxiliary blower.
The drive's non-sinusoidal output has effects on the motor: more losses, poor ventilation at low speed, stress on winding insulation, noise and shaft currents.
Power depends on the load: on a constant-torque load input power varies linearly with speed, whereas a fan at half speed needs only one eighth of full-load power.
Soft starting and stopping avoids mechanical jolts that damage belts, gears and bearings.
Compared with a direct start or star-delta, a drive is the only option when motor speed control is needed.
On a cabinet drive the main switch on the door does not remove the voltage from the input busbars, so isolate the whole drive from the supply before work (added for i3's safe isolation).
One single-phase winding makes a pulsating field, not a turning one, so it gives no starting torque; a three-phase motor on one phase will not self-start but can be hand started either way.

A start winding at 90 electrical degrees, with thinner wire and fewer turns, has higher resistance and lower inductance, so its current shifts less than the main winding's; the two currents are out of step and the field turns.
The angle between the two currents in a split-phase motor is about 30 degrees.
Starting torque goes with the currents and the sine of the angle between them.
A centrifugal switch drops the start winding out: at 3/4 of synchronous speed (Kuphaldt), about 75% of running speed (his sheet), approximately 80% of full speed (MSU).

Split-phase starting torque is low and suits easily started loads and fractional horsepower, up to 1/3 horsepower (250 W); typical figures are 100 to 175% of rated torque and 700 to 1,000% of rated current.
The start winding is not rated for continuous use, so frequent starts or a long start can overheat and burn it out.
Once started the auxiliary winding is optional; the main winding alone keeps the motor running.
The direction is set by reversing the leads of one winding (start or main) before starting.

During the start period the two windings are in parallel across the supply, on separate poles 90 electrical degrees apart. The start winding has fewer turns of finer wire (higher resistance) sitting nearer the slot surface (lower inductance), so its current is closer to in step with the supply voltage than the main winding's.

The angle between the two currents is small, about 30 degrees, but enough to give a weak rotating field. Sources differ on its size: about 30 degrees (Kuphaldt, IDC, PEG-3722), about half of the ideal 90 (a textbook), and 25 degrees in one university worked example (currents 40 and 15 degrees behind the supply).
notes.contested: How big the split-phase angle is: Kuphaldt, IDC and PEG-3722 say about 30 degrees; Goodheart-Willcox says about half of 90; Utah's worked example has 25 (40 and 15 degrees behind the supply). The lesson uses a labelled example value.

notes.claim: A worked example to compute from: a 1/3 hp, 120 V split-phase motor draws 5 A in the main winding and 3 A in the start winding on switching on, the currents 40 and 15 degrees behind the supply voltage (Utah ECE 3600 Ex. 1).

The centrifugal switch holds the start-winding contacts closed at rest. The flyweights open them as the rotor reaches about 75 to 80 percent of speed, and let them close again as the motor slows, ready for the next start. It protects the start winding from destructive overload.
The torque falls at the speed where the start winding drops out, and the main winding carries on alone.

The start winding and capacitor are not rated for continuous duty. Frequent starts leave too little cooling time and the winding overheats: its current density is so high while starting that the temperature rise rules out frequent restarting or slow-starting loads. Start-winding failure is a common failure point of single-phase motors.

Split-phase starting torque and current: roughly 100 to 175 percent of rated torque at 500 to 800 percent of rated current (a study guide), against 700 to 1,000 percent of rated current in Microchip's note; the figures differ by source, so the lesson gives a range or a labelled example.
notes.contested: Split-phase starting current: Microchip says 700 to 1,000 percent of rated, a study guide says 500 to 800 percent.

notes.claim: Start circuit open (switch stuck open or failing to close, open start winding): the motor hums and will not start; the run winding draws near locked-rotor current until the overload trips or heat damages it. A single winding cannot start the rotor, but once it is turning it develops torque, in whichever direction it was started.
Switch stuck closed (contacts stuck together): the start winding stays energized, overheats and burns, and the motor trips on overload.
Diagnostic aids: a working centrifugal switch clicks almost at once on starting and again as the rotor slows after switching off, so no click suggests a faulty switch.
A centrifugal switch cannot be used in explosive atmospheres or inside hermetic compressors, because the arcing from switching can ignite gases.

Testing, with the motor isolated and locked off first: an ohmmeter across the motor's supply terminals reads the two windings in parallel, so less than either alone; zero is a short, infinity an open circuit; operating the centrifugal switch by hand should change the reading. Three-terminal check (stated for compressor motors with the same winding layout): start-to-common is typically three to five times run-to-common, and common-to-start plus common-to-run equals run-to-start.
A motor with a thermal protector that resets itself can restart at any time, so isolate it before touching it.
Reversing a single-phase motor: interchange the leads of the start winding relative to the run winding, not the supply leads.
A capacitor in series with the start winding makes that winding's current lead the supply voltage, while the main winding's current still lags, so the angle between the currents grows.
The angle is almost 80 degrees against about 30 degrees in a split-phase motor; ideally the capacitor is chosen so the start winding's current leads the main winding's by 90 degrees at startup.
Starting torque goes with the sine of the angle between the currents, so going from 30 to 80 degrees alone raises starting torque to nearly twice that of a split-phase motor.
A capacitor-start motor has moderate starting torque, higher than split-phase, and the phase shift is greater.
The centrifugal switch takes the start winding and capacitor out at about 75 to 80% of speed.
The motor then runs on the main winding alone. His sheet credits 'momentum from the startup'; the fuller source says the auxiliary winding is optional once started.
A permanent-split capacitor motor keeps a continuously energised auxiliary winding and has no centrifugal switch; a larger capacitor can be used just for starting if switched out at speed.
A failed capacitor is one of the most common causes of a motor that hums but will not start; compare a measured capacitor value with its marked rating.
The capacitor is chosen so the start winding's current leads the main winding's by close to 90 degrees; the two windings then act like a two-phase stator and make the turning field.

Starting torque goes with both winding currents and the sine of the angle between them, so a capacitor that gives exactly 90 degrees is not automatically the one that gives the most torque; the capacitor value also changes the start winding's current.

A capacitor-start motor gives roughly three times full-load torque at start in one maker's figures, more than double a split-phase motor's starting torque with about a third less starting current in an open textbook, and better starting torque with lower starting current in the USNRC manual; figures differ between sources, so the lesson treats them as typical, not exact.

The angle between the winding currents is about 80 degrees in a capacitor-start motor against about 25 degrees in the same text's split-phase motor (30 degrees in other sources); the sources differ on the split-phase figure.

The ideal 90 degrees holds at one speed only: a worked example sizes the capacitor for startup, and a different value (28.4 microfarads in the same notes' problem) gives 90 degrees at rated speed. Utah's own worked example for a 1/3 hp 120 V split-phase motor adds a capacitor to reach 90 degrees and the start winding current falls to about 2 A.

The start capacitor is a dry electrolytic type not rated for continuous duty, usable only for intermittent duty (1 second on, 60 seconds off), and the switch removes it with the auxiliary winding near full speed; starting often overheats the capacitor and it fails.
Once the switch has opened the motor runs as a plain single-phase induction motor on its main winding; this is not momentum from the start.
Capacitor-start motors suit hard-to-start loads such as compressors, pumps and conveyors, and loads where the starting period may be long.

A capacitor-start capacitor-run motor starts with a large capacitor and keeps a smaller one in circuit to improve running; it has lower full-load current and is used on most higher horsepower single-phase motors. A permanent split capacitor motor has low starting torque and low starting current and has no centrifugal switch.
A capacitor that opens or deteriorates leaves poor starting torque, which may stop the motor starting and usually trips the overloads; a capacitor that short-circuits may burn out the winding.

Checking a start capacitor: switch off and prove dead, then discharge it through a resistor (20 kilohm, 5 W for about five seconds), measure its capacitance and compare with the value marked on it; look for a bulging top, leaking oil, or a cracked or scorched case. The allowed tolerance differs between sources (plus or minus 20% or 10% for a start capacitor).

A capacitor-start motor from the US Navy training series is described the same way: a starting winding and a capacitor in series, currents nearly 90 degrees apart, and a centrifugal switch that cuts out the starting winding near full speed.

For i5 (why it keeps running on one winding): a single winding's pulsating field can be seen as two counter-rotating fields. Once the rotor turns, it develops torque from the field turning its way and little from the other, so torque, not momentum, keeps it running.
In a series motor the same current flows through field and armature.

A turning armature makes a back emf opposing the supply; it is zero at standstill, so a motor not yet turning draws maximum current, and a load that slows it drops the back emf and raises the current.
The armature current is limited at start by armature resistance alone, so an external starting resistance is placed in series with the armature.
The motor's back emf is the supply voltage less the voltage lost in the resistance.
In its linear (unsaturated) region a series motor's torque goes with the square of the armature current, so it has very high starting torque.
Remove the load and the current falls, the field weakens, and the speed rises towards destruction: series motors must have overspeed protection and be coupled directly, never belt driven.
A shunt or compound motor can be run safely with no load but a series motor cannot.
A series motor suits crane hoists, elevators and large excavators, where a high starting torque is crucial.
A universal motor can operate on either AC or DC power and uses an electromagnet as its stator.

Starting current is supply voltage over armature resistance. Worked case: a 10 hp motor, 0.4 ohm armature, 260 V would draw 650 A, about twelve times full load; a 0.5 ohm, 220 V, 7.5 kW motor draws 440 A against 34 A. Guides for the limit differ (125 to 200 percent, or two to three times full-load current), so teach a range.

Armature resistance is low (0.05 to 0.5 ohm for most motor armatures), and counter emf does not exist until the armature turns, so an external starting resistance goes in series with the armature to keep the first current safe.

Series motor laws: below saturation flux follows current, so speed goes with 1 over current (very small current gives dangerous speed). After saturation flux is fixed and torque goes only with current, so the square law holds only below saturation. Starting torque is exceptionally high; railway locomotives are the classic user.
Reversing: reverse the armature or the field connections, not both. Reversing the supply reverses both, so direction is unchanged.
On AC, a plain DC series motor with a laminated field has its field current cut by the field coil reactance, so it runs poorly; small universal motors are built for either supply.

The series-motor starter is a two-point starter with a no-load release (hold-on) coil in series with the armature: if the load is lost the current falls, the coil lets go and the arm springs back to OFF, preventing overspeed. It also drops out on voltage loss.

Naval and marine, dated: US Navy training text says dc motors suit winches, cranes and missile launchers; its series field is a few turns of large wire carrying full armature current. A 1907 US Navy text uses series motors for boat cranes and winches and says gear and motor losses were thought enough to prevent racing: old practice, against modern advice to fit overspeed protection.

Engine cranking: diesel locomotives crank with two 32 V series-wound motors in series from a 64 V battery; engine inertia lets current and torque reach extreme levels before counter emf builds (locomotive, not marine).

Faults and tests (isolate and prove dead first): brush and commutator wear causes sparking; megger windings to frame; measure armature and field winding resistance (open circuits, shorted turns); no start can come from an open field, grounded leads or poor brush contact.
Universal motors are series-wound motors that run on AC or DC; portable power tools such as angle grinders use them (for i6: the grinder as a series motor Dan has used).
In a shunt motor the field is across the supply, so its current and flux stay steady.
A heavier load slows the motor, which lowers the back emf, lets more armature current flow and raises the torque; the speed settles a little lower than before.
His sheet says the extra current makes the motor 'speed back up to compensate'; the fuller sources say the speed falls off as the load increases.
notes.contested: Dan's sheet says a loaded shunt motor speeds back up to compensate; textbooks say its speed is nearly constant but falls off as load increases.

notes.claim: Speed regulation is the change in speed from no load to full load divided by the full-load speed; sources differ: his sheet 10 to 20%, IDC 7 to 10%, one site puts the armature drop at about 5%.
notes.contested: Sources differ on how far a shunt motor's speed falls between no load and full load: 10-20% (his sheet), 7-10% (IDC), about 5% (a circuits site).

notes.claim: Weakening the field raises the speed: a rheostat in series with the shunt field gives speeds above rated, and is the usual method.
Start a shunt motor with the field rheostat in the slow-speed position, so the field current is at its maximum: starting torque goes with field current.
Lower starting torque than a series motor: his sheet and a text say so, while Rose-Hulman says the starting torque is as high as in the series motor.
notes.contested: Whether a shunt motor's starting torque is lower than a series motor's: his sheet and PEG-3722 say lower; Rose-Hulman says as high.

notes.claim: A shunt motor has a safe no-load speed as long as the field is not de-energised; if the field fails the speed can run away, so loss-of-field protection is usual.
Brushes and commutator need regular maintenance.
Shunt motors suit constant-speed work such as machine tools and pumps.

The supply voltage is shared between the back emf and the drop across the armature: V = Eb + Ia Ra, so Ia = (V - Eb) / Ra; the field current is a separate branch (It = Ia + If). Back emf is proportional to flux times speed.

Why the armature current follows the load: put the load on and the armature slows; the I x R drop takes a bigger share of the supply, so less back emf is needed, and the armature current and torque climb until they match the load.

Torque is proportional to flux times armature current; in a shunt motor the flux is practically constant, so torque is proportional to Ia. Speed is proportional to the supply voltage over the field flux.

Speed regulation is defined by the standard as the no-load speed minus the rated-load speed, as a percent of rated-load speed, and a dc shunt-wound motor is named as an example of a constant-speed motor.

How far a shunt motor's speed falls from no load to full load: two industry guides give 5 to 10%, his sheet gives 10 to 20%, and the armature drop alone gives about 4 to 5% (the lesson computes about 4% from the cited Rose-Hulman example). The IDC '7 to 10%' figure sits under IDC's Ward-Leonard heading (the sentence before it says the driving motor's speed is set by varying the voltage applied to the armature with a generator), so it is a figure for that system, not for a plain shunt motor on a fixed supply.
notes.contested: How far a shunt motor's speed falls from no load to full load: his sheet says 10-20%; two industry guides say 5-10%; the armature drop alone gives about 4-5%. IDC's 7-10% belongs to Ward-Leonard control, not to a plain shunt motor.

notes.claim: A cited worked example the lesson can use for its numbers: a DC shunt motor rated 600 V, 255 hp, 2000 rpm, armature resistance 0.07 ohm, total field resistance 80 ohm, drawing 353 A at rated load. The lesson computes the rest from these: field current 7.5 A, armature current 345.5 A, back emf 575.8 V, and the speed at other loads from speed proportional to back emf at constant flux (see i7.examples.json).

Whether the speed falls or rises as load goes on: the resistance drop gives a slight fall, and textbooks say so; but armature reaction weakens the flux and can make a plain 'straight shunt' motor's speed rise with load, so makers add a light series winding (stabilised shunt) to make the speed droop. His sheet says the motor speeds back up to compensate.
notes.contested: Does a loaded shunt motor's speed fall or rise? The usual rule is a slight fall; a plain straight shunt motor can rise because of armature reaction (so makers add a stabilising series winding); his sheet says it speeds back up to compensate.

notes.claim: Shunt motors suit work where the speed must stay near the set point as the load changes: pumps, fans, blowers, conveyors, machine tools and printing. The drawback noted is low starting torque.

Starting torque: a maker-neutral guide gives about 250% for a shunt machine against up to 500% for a series machine, and another says a shunt motor can deliver 300% of full-load torque for a very short time. This supports his sheet (lower than a series motor) and not Rose-Hulman's 'as high as in the series motor'.
notes.contested: Whether a shunt motor's starting torque is lower than a series motor's: his sheet, PEG-3722, MSU and Motordoc (about 250% against up to 500%) say lower; Rose-Hulman says as high.

notes.claim: Speed control in two ranges: below base speed lower the armature voltage (constant torque), above base speed weaken the field (constant power). A motor with 1750 rpm base speed on 500 V runs at 875 rpm on 250 V. Making the field stronger than rated to go slower is not allowed because the field overheats.

The field rheostat is the preferred way to adjust speed because the field current is much smaller than the armature current, so less power is lost in the rheostat; a rheostat in the armature circuit wastes more power and only lowers the speed.

Limits of field weakening: a maker winds its stock 180 V motors as plain straight shunt only for a field-weakened speed up to 105% of base speed, always keeps the speed within the maximum safe speed on the nameplate, and warns that a field-weakened motor can exceed safe speed at light load.

Starting: with no back emf at standstill only the armature resistance limits the current (a 10 hp, 0.4 ohm armature on 260 V would take 650 A, about twelve times full load); starting resistors limit it to 125 to 200 percent of full-load current. Start with the field rheostat at the slow-speed position (full field); many starters interlock the speed regulator so the motor cannot start on a weak field.
The faceplate starter: the handle is held by the no-volt coil and springs back to off if the supply fails; the overload coil short-circuits the no-volt coil on overload, so the handle is released.

Three-point and four-point starters: in a three-point starter the no-volt coil is in series with the shunt field, so it also protects against an open field; but weakening the field for speed can let the coil drop out. In a four-point starter the coil is across the supply, which frees the speed control but loses the open-field protection.

Field failure: with little or no load, losing the field supply makes the speed rise a great deal (a runaway) and damages the motor; a loss-of-field relay (device 40) is the protection named for shunt-wound DC motors, and Rose-Hulman says loss-of-field protection is usual.
notes.contested: What an open field does: with little or no load the speed runs away (MSU, Rose-Hulman, his sheet); PEG-3722 says the motor tends to keep running on residual magnetism. Both follow speed = back emf / flux: how fast depends on the load and the residual flux.

notes.claim: Residual magnetism in the poles keeps a weak field after the field winding is disconnected, and the armature keeps drawing current from the supply.
Reversing: swap either the armature leads or the field leads (not both); reversing both leaves the direction unchanged.
Lowering the field current weakens the flux, and the rotor speeds up to make the back emf the circuit needs.

Faults and tests (isolate and prove dead first): brushes and commutator are wear parts and dust collects inside; the basic checks are insulation resistance and circuit (winding) resistance; sparking at the brushes can come from the armature winding; a commutator is inspected for roughness, loose bars, uneven bar height and mica; insulation resistance of armature and field windings is covered by IEEE Std 43.

Marine and drive context: a maker lists DC motors suitable for IEEE 45 shipboard applications; a US Coast Guard specification covers DC propulsion generators and motors; shunt-wound motors pair well with SCR drives; AC drives have reduced DC machines in new large installations.

For i7 (where it is used): AC drives have taken market share from DC drives, mainly because a DC motor's brushes need regular maintenance and its commutator complicates the motor and consumes energy; a link back to lesson 3, the VSD.
A compound motor has both a series and a shunt field winding.
In a cumulative compound motor the series and shunt fields work together, with fluxes in the same direction; in a differential one they oppose.
A shunt coil added to a series motor limits the top speed at light load, and a cumulative compound motor has a definite no-load speed and can run safely with no load.
A cumulative compound motor has more starting torque than a shunt motor and steadier speed than a series motor, but not as steady as a shunt motor.
A differential compound motor is rarely used because it can run unstably when the load changes; because the series flux opposes the shunt flux, flux falls with load and the speed can rise with load.
A long-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the supply with the series winding between it and the armature; a short-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the armature only.
Compound motors suit presses, shears, crushers and reciprocating compressors.

NEMA defines a compound-wound motor as a direct-current motor with two separate field windings: one, usually the predominating field, connected as in a straight shunt-wound motor, and the other connected in series with the armature circuit.

Percent compounding is the share of the total field ampere-turns at full load that the series field contributes (NEMA). A stabilised-shunt motor takes about 3 to 10 percent from its series winding; one trade source says a typical industrial compound motor takes about 50 percent.

CONTESTED share: computed from the lesson's flux rule, a 50 percent series share would double the no-load speed, far outside the 15 to 30 percent speed regulation makers quote. The lesson uses a labelled example share (i8.examples.json) and does not teach 50 percent as a fact.

Flux rule for the picture: in a cumulative compound motor the series winding adds flux as the load current rises, so flux = shunt part + series part x armature current; in a differential one the series part is taken away (net flux falls with load). Speed follows applied voltage minus the armature-circuit drop, divided by net flux.

Cumulative: the series part supplies a large torque when the motor is started under a heavy load and the shunt part gives the constant-speed advantage of a shunt motor (US Navy training text). A compound motor has more torque than a shunt motor because of the series field, with a fairly constant speed because of the shunt field (DOE Fundamentals Handbook); it copes with heavy load changes better than a shunt motor because the extra current in the series coils strengthens the field (university notes).

Speed regulation of a cumulative compound motor is poorer than a shunt motor's: a load makes the speed fall further because the flux grows with load (PEG-3722; Engineers Edge says 'less speed regulation'). NEMA defines speed regulation as no-load minus rated-load speed, in percent of rated-load speed.

Makers' figures for a standard compound motor's speed regulation: about 30 percent (Baldor-Reliance, quoting NEMA MG1 12.65.2) and 15 to 25 percent (another Baldor-Reliance frame range). CONTESTED against his sheet, which says 'good speed regulation (like a shunt motor)': teach it as better than a series motor and worse than a shunt motor.

A compound motor is not suited to speed control by weakening its shunt field, because of the very high no-load speeds that can result (Baldor-Reliance). Its shunt part gives it a definite no-load speed and keeps it from running uncontrollably when the load goes (PEG-3722, existing sources 165 and 192).

Differential compound: the series field opposes the shunt field, so the net flux falls with load and the speed rises as the load increases, which may lead to instability. A heavy enough load can take the flux to zero so the machine stalls or reverses. It is rarely used (his sheet, existing source 190).

CONTESTED detail: PEG-3722 and Engineers Edge describe a differential motor as running at a constant speed with better regulation than a shunt motor. Both follow flux = shunt part - series part x current: a small series part only cancels the usual speed droop (flat), a large one makes the speed rise. The lesson teaches it as unstable (the sheet) and shows the rise in red.

Reversing the series field alone (or the shunt field alone) turns cumulative into differential; reversing both fields together does not change whether they aid or oppose. To reverse the direction of rotation of a compound motor, reverse the armature leads, or reverse both fields. A maker winds a motor as a straight shunt for regenerative drives, because the series winding would oppose the shunt winding when the motor is reversed or regenerates.

Fault to find after a repair or rebuild: a speed that climbs as armature current climbs points to a hidden differential series winding (a rebuild can reverse an internal series field), reversed interpole polarity or brushes off neutral. Check against the maker's connection diagram.

Safety and weight of evidence: do not find out the polarity by running the motor unloaded at normal voltage, because weak or opposing flux can allow excessive speed. One trade note adds that under high starting current a differentially connected series winding can overpower the shunt field and drive the motor the wrong way; one trade source only, so the lesson may say 'can' and no more.

Why a flywheel goes with a compound motor on a press or shear: the machine takes its working energy during the work stroke from the flywheel and the motor then brings the flywheel back to rated speed; flywheel kinetic energy is proportional to the square of its speed (Yaskawa; a university thesis says the same of the motor between punches).

A compound motor is generally used with a flywheel where sudden, temporary loads come on, as in rolling mills: the series winding takes the heavy load and the shunt winding stops dangerous speed when the load is suddenly removed. NO SOURCE says the speed droop is what lets the flywheel give up its energy; that follows from energy proportional to speed squared and is the lesson's own computed reasoning (i8.examples.json), said as such.

Uses: presses, shears and reciprocating machines are often driven by compounded motors (DOE Fundamentals Handbook; his sheet, existing source 201); a compound motor suits a reciprocating press or shear where a relatively consistent speed is wanted with irregular loads.

Long and short shunt (existing sources 199, 200): the lesson's drawing of his sheet is long shunt (shunt winding across the supply, series winding between it and the armature). Source gap: no source states the short-shunt current rule in quotable words, so the picture uses long shunt only.

Marine and naval line: the only support found is a US Navy training text (NEETS) describing the compound motor as one shunt winding in parallel with the armature and one series winding in series with it, with the speed and torque characteristics a combination of series and shunt motors. NO source was found that places a compound motor on a ship or names a shipboard compound-motor service, so the lesson carries no marine use line for the compound motor.

Example-set note: one worked tutorial uses a flux that changes by 0.4 percent for each ampere of armature current (240 V, 0.20 ohm). That is an example value, not a maker's; the lesson uses its own labelled per-unit set (i8.examples.json).
